title.en: The Vineyards Above Manarola: A Winemaker's Year

body.title: The Vineyards Above Manarola: A Winemaker's Year
body.subtitle: Where the rhythm of the seasons is measured in pruning shears, hand-carried water, and the weight of a harvest basket

body.badge: The Land & Those Who Tend It
body.quote: Every stone in these walls was carried up on someone's back. Every vine knows the hands that prune it.
body.leftContent:
Above Manarola, the hillside rises in geometric defiance of gravity. Narrow terraces climb toward the sky, held in place by muretti a secco — dry-stone walls built without mortar, fitted so precisely that centuries of rain and wind have barely shifted them. The vines that grow here are small, gnarled, their roots searching through thin soil for purchase in the schist below.

This is not gentle farming country. The slopes are too steep for machines. The sun too relentless in summer, the winter winds too sharp. Everything that happens here happens by hand, or not at all.
body.rightContent:
I spent a year following the rhythm of these vineyards, watching one winemaker's calendar unfold. Not because any single season tells the whole story, but because the seasons here repeat themselves with such fidelity that to understand one spring is to understand them all.

What I learned: the wine you taste in a glass of Sciacchetrà is inseparable from the labor that made it. Every golden drop is a small archive of human effort, of decisions made on cold January mornings and August afternoons when the air shimmers with heat.

body.markdown: Spring arrives quietly in the vineyards. Late March, early April — the exact timing depends on the winter just past, on whether the tramontana winds were harsh or mild. You wake one morning and the air smells different: damp earth warming, the faint citrus sweetness of lemon blossoms from the groves that cling to pockets of deeper soil between the vine terraces.

This is pruning season, the most contemplative work of the year. Each vine must be read like a text — which canes produced well last year, which should be cut back, where the energy of the plant wants to go. The pruning shears make a clean, rhythmic snick as they work through wood. The cuttings are bundled and carried down the hillside, used later for grafting or burned for heat. Nothing is wasted here. Nothing can afford to be.

By May, the vines wake. Tiny green shoots uncurl from the old wood, and suddenly the hillside that was gray and brown all winter turns soft with new growth. The first leaves are tender, almost translucent when the sun catches them. This is when the real attentiveness begins — checking for frost (rare but catastrophic), watching for early signs of disease, thinning shoots so the plant's energy flows where you want it.

body.alt: Stone-walled vineyard terraces winding through coastal hills at golden hour
body.caption: The terraces above Manarola, where every stone wall tells a story of patient labor. Photo by Evgeni Tcherkasski on Unsplash

body.markdown: Summer is when the vineyards demand everything. June, July, August — the sun climbs high and stays there, baking the terraces until the stones radiate heat well into the evening. The grapes swell and change color, a process the old-timers call invaiatura. Bosco grapes develop their golden-green hue, Albarola turns pale yellow, Vermentino takes on a slightly darker amber when left to ripen fully.

Water is the constant negotiation. There's no irrigation system on these old terraces, nothing but what the sky provides and what can be carried up by hand or on the narrow-gauge trenini — the little monorail tracks that snake up the steepest slopes, carrying tools, sulfur for treating the vines, jerry cans of water on the hottest days. The cicadas sing their relentless drone. You work early in the morning or late in the evening, when the heat backs off enough to breathe.

The grapes are thinned in July — cutting away clusters that won't ripen properly, ensuring the vines put their diminishing energy into fewer, better fruit. It feels wasteful the first time you do it, dropping perfectly good grapes onto the ground. But the wine will tell you later that it was necessary.

Autumn is vendemmia — harvest time. Late September usually, sometimes early October if the weather has been cool. The exact day is determined by sugar content in the grapes, measured with a refractometer, and by taste. You walk the terraces, sampling grapes from different sections, feeling the balance between sugar and acid, sensing when they've reached that perfect ripeness.

Then the call goes out. Vendemmia begins with the rising sun, often with borrowed hands — neighbors, family, anyone who can carry a basket and isn't afraid of steep paths. The grapes are cut cluster by cluster, laid carefully into shallow baskets so they don't crush under their own weight. The full baskets go onto the trenini or onto shoulders for the steep sections where even the rail can't go.

By mid-morning, your back aches, your fingers are sticky with juice, and your legs have remembered every single stone step on the path. By midday, you break for focaccia and cold white wine — never Sciacchetrà during harvest, that's far too precious — and someone tells the same stories they told last year, about the vendemmia of 1987 or 2003, the legendary years that everyone measures against.

By evening, the terraces are stripped, and the work moves to the cantina. The air is rich with the smell of crushed grapes, that particular sweetness that's both fruity and fermented at once. The Bosco and Albarola destined for Sciacchetrà are laid out on racks to dry — appassimento, the slow raisining that concentrates their sugars and flavors.

body.quote: I was eight the first time I helped with vendemmia, and what I remember most is the weight of the basket. Not just the physical weight of the grapes, but the way it seemed to contain everything — the sun, the work of months, my grandmother's careful hands selecting each cluster. And I remember how the sea below us changed as the day moved: flat silver in the morning, deep blue by noon, then gold as the afternoon light slanted across it. The terraces taught me that beauty and labor aren't opposites. They're the same thing, seen from different angles.
body.author: Giulia Rossi

body.markdown: Winter in the vineyards is a season of silence and patience. The vines are bare, their dark canes stark against the stone walls. The work slows but never stops — there's always maintenance on the muretti, stones to re-fit where frost has shifted them, repairs to the trenini tracks, planning for the spring pruning.

And in the cantina, the Sciacchetrà is slowly becoming itself. The dried grapes — now deeply concentrated, almost like raisins — are finally pressed in November or December. The must is thick, golden, impossibly sweet. It ferments slowly through the winter, sometimes into spring, the yeast working through all that sugar in its own time.

This is why Sciacchetrà costs what it does. Not because of marketing or mystique, but because of mathematics. A vine that might produce a bottle of regular wine will produce maybe a glass of Sciacchetrà. The grapes must be perfect — no disease, no damage — because they'll spend weeks drying, and any flaw will intensify. The yield is tiny. The labor is enormous. A single bottle might represent forty or fifty hours of human work, spread across a full year.

When you taste it — that honeyed, complex amber wine with flavors of apricot and walnut and the sea air that flavored the grapes as they grew — you're tasting a year in the life of a terraced hillside. You're tasting the spring pruning decisions, the summer heat management, the careful harvest timing, the patient waiting of winter. You're tasting the muretti a secco holding the soil in place, the trenini carrying water up impossible slopes, the hands sorting grapes by candlelight.
Every glass is a small archive of human effort. Every sip is a year compressed into liquid. This is what it means to make wine on the vertical edge of the sea.

body.title: Walk Slowly Above Manarola
body.content:
The terraces above Manarola are crisscrossed with paths — ancient trails that connect the vineyards to the village below and the sanctuary of Volastra above. Many of them are open to walkers, though you should stay on the marked trails and respect the fact that these are working landscapes, not museums.

When you walk these paths, you're doing something more than sightseeing. You're participating in an act of preservation. Every visitor who understands what these terraces represent — what they cost in labor, what they mean culturally — becomes a small advocate for their survival. In a world that increasingly values efficiency and mechanization, these vineyards are an argument for the opposite: for slowness, for human scale, for the kind of quality that can only come from intimate knowledge and patient work.

The winemakers here aren't performing tradition for tourists. They're living it because it's the only way to make this particular wine, in this particular place. And as long as people keep understanding that — keep tasting the difference, keep valuing the labor — the muretti will keep standing, and the spring pruning will happen on schedule, and the vendemmia will call neighbors together on golden September mornings.
